title: London's Wellcome Collection Returns 2,000 Sacred Jain Manuscripts in Landmark Restitution
excerpt: The largest collection of Jain texts outside South Asia will move to the University of Birmingham, giving Britain's 30,000 Jains direct access to their heritage for the first time
body:
## A Century-Old Debt Repaid

In a wood-panelled committee room in the House of Commons, representatives from London's Wellcome Collection and the Institute of Jainology signed what both sides called a landmark agreement: the return of more than 2,000 sacred Jain manuscripts — the largest such collection outside South Asia — to the community from which they were taken over a century ago.

The manuscripts, most dating to the fifteenth century, cover an extraordinary range of subjects: Jain theology and cosmology, classical Indian literature, Ayurvedic medicine, mathematics, and astronomy. Among them are rare copies of the **Kalpasutra**, one of the most revered texts in the Jain canon, describing the lives of the *tirthankaras*. Many were found still wrapped in the 1919 Indian newspapers in which they had been packed when the Wellcome Trust first acquired them.

### How They Got to London

The collection arrived in Britain in 1919, purchased at a low price from what is now Pakistan — years before the Partition that would scatter Jain communities across the subcontinent. Sir Henry Wellcome, the pharmaceutical magnate whose collections formed the basis of the Wellcome Trust, was an avid buyer of medical texts and curiosities. The manuscripts were absorbed into a vast library and, for decades, stored rather than studied.

The Wellcome Collection has now acknowledged that the acquisition was ethically troubling by the standards of its own era and indefensible by today's. "These manuscripts belong with the community that created them and holds them sacred," said the museum in a statement accompanying the signing.

### A New Home — But Not India

In a decision that underscores the complexity of cultural restitution, the manuscripts will not return to South Asia. Instead, they will be transferred to the **University of Birmingham**, where the newly established **Dharmanath Network in Jain Studies** will house, conserve, and digitise them. The arrangement, brokered by the **Institute of Jainology**, ensures the collection remains accessible to the estimated 30,000 Jains living in the United Kingdom — a community that traces its British roots to the East African diaspora waves of the 1960s and 1970s.

For Jains in the UK, the return carries emotional weight that extends beyond scholarship. The manuscripts represent a continuous intellectual tradition stretching back millennia, one that survived Mughal invasions, colonial extraction, and the upheaval of Partition. Their new home in Birmingham — already a centre of South Asian academic life — is intended to serve as both a research hub and a place of community access.

### What It Means for the Diaspora

The agreement arrives during a broader global reckoning over colonial-era acquisitions. In the same week, the Netherlands repatriated eleventh-century Chola-era copper plates to India during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to The Hague. Museums from New York to Amsterdam are reviewing their own holdings under mounting pressure from source communities.

For NRIs and PIOs in the UK, the Jain manuscripts case offers a different model: restitution that keeps artefacts close to the diaspora communities who can engage with them daily, rather than sending them to national museums thousands of miles from the people who most value them. Whether that model satisfies all stakeholders — including voices in India who argue the manuscripts belong on the subcontinent — remains an open question.

What is not in question is the significance of the moment. After more than a century in storage, 2,000 manuscripts will be read, studied, and revered again — not as museum curiosities, but as the living heritage they were always meant to be.
